implementation_notes: The runtime already supplies the facade for OS handles: derive from SafeHandle (usually SafeHandleZeroOrMinusOneIsInvalid), override ReleaseHandle, and let P/Invoke marshal the type - it keeps the handle alive across the native call and frees it exactly once through Dispose, with a critical finalizer as backstop. Prefer the shipped handles (SafeFileHandle, SafeProcessHandle, SafeWaitHandle) and the BCL streams and clients (FileStream, HttpClient) over an IntPtr-based wrapper, which leaks on asynchronous exceptions.
pitfalls: An IntPtr handle in a wrapper's field is reclaimed by the GC at an unpredictable moment: without SafeHandle the finalizer can free the handle while a native call is still running.
ReleaseHandle runs in a constrained execution region under critical finalization: it must not throw and must not allocate its way into failure.
Passing a SafeHandle with ownsHandle: false to a type that closes it anyway double-frees the native handle.

variants.name: Source-generated interop (LibraryImport)
variants.implementation_notes: The same SafeHandle facade, but the marshalling layer is generated at compile time by the LibraryImport source generator instead of being constructed by runtime P/Invoke: the partial method declaration is expanded into strongly typed, trimming- and AOT-friendly marshalling code. C# 11 is the floor because the generator relies on that language level. The facade's shape does not change - a class owns a SafeHandle-derived type and exposes intent-named methods - only how the native call is emitted.
pitfalls: Generated marshalling is compile-time: a binding that compiles for one architecture still has to be validated for the native library's own struct layouts and calling convention.
The generator requires unsafe or partial-type plumbing and C# 11; older compilers silently keep using the runtime marshaller.
Both interop forms still require a SafeHandle-derived type for the handle itself - generated code does not add lifetime safety by itself.
